background.definition: Motion sickness is the discomfort experienced when perceived motion disturbs the organs of balance.

list.listitem: Motion sickness is rare in children younger than 2 years of age, and its incidence peaks between the ages of 3 and 12.
It is more common in women and persons with a history of migraine headache.
An estimated one-third of the population is highly susceptible to motion sickness.
Under extreme conditions virtually 100% of the population will experience motion sickness.
Multiple theories regarding the cause of motion sickness exist; researchers have been unable to agree on one unifying theory.
A functional vestibular system is a prerequisite for motion sickness to occur.

Central cholinergic synapses use acetylcholine to transmit motion information from the vestibular end organs; sympathetic synapses, using dopamine, epinephrine, or norepinephrine antagonize this neuronal transmission.
Vision is not essential to motion sickness; blind inviduals can still be susceptible.
Nausea, vomiting, pallor, cold sweats, hypersalivation, hyperventilation, and/or headaches after exposure to motion stimulus strongly suggest motion sickness. C
A history of vomiting is not necessary, however, to make the diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Occurs with rapid, momentary change in head position; abnormal Dix-Hallpike maneuver
Simultaneous migraine headache with the absence of motion stimulus
Vomiting with sensation of rotational vertigo at rest; associated tinnitus
Commonly occurs after otitis media; associated loss of balance and tinnitus
Progressive unilateral hearing loss and/or tinnitus

list.listitem: A history of any combination of the following symptoms after exposure to motion stimulus (e.g., automobile, airplane, boat, space ship) is strongly suggestive of motion sickness: nausea, vomiting, pallor, cold sweats, hypersalivation, hyperventilation, and headaches.
A history of vomiting after exposure to motion stimulus, however, is not necessary to make the diagnosis; many individuals who suffer significant motion sickness never vomit.

The physical exam should focus on ruling out other conditions; no single parameter has been found to be of high enough sensitivity and specificity for the diagnosis or prediction of individual motion sickness susceptibility.
No diagnostic instrument is currently available to clinicians to confirm or refute the diagnosis of motion sickness.

Proceed with empiric treatment if the clinical history and exam are consistent with motion sickness; expected symptoms should occur only with or immediately following exposure to motion stimulus, and physical examination in the office should be unremarkable.
Symptoms that occur in the absence of motion stimulus or any abnormal findings on physical examination should prompt evaluation for an alternative cause (see Differential diagnosis).
See algorithm in .
Scopolamine prevents motion sickness symptoms in susceptible individuals. A
Dimenhydrinate, meclizine, and promethazine are commonly prescribed to prevent motion sickness symptoms in susceptible individuals. C

A Cochrane review of 14 RCTs with 1025 subjects found that scoploamine (transdermal, tablet, capsule, oral solution, or intravenous formulation) effectively prevents motion sickness. Its common side effects include dry mouth and drowsiness.

Although no recent RCTs demonstrate their effectiveness, dimenhydrinate (Dramamine), meclizine, and promethazine have each been in common use for motion sickness for over 40 years. All three can cause significant drowsiness. A small RCT (n = 18) found that chlorpheniramine was effective at preventing motion sickness.
A small RCT (n = 10) demonstrated that rizatriptan prevented motion sickness symptoms in migraineurs who have a history of motion sickness.
Studies show conflicting evidence regarding the effectiveness of ginger.
Studies show conflicting evidence regarding the effectiveness of acupressure/acupuncture.
One RCT demonstrated that a high-protein meal may attenuate nausea in motion sick subjects.
A controlled breathing regimen effectively reduces motion sickness symptoms, but the length of required training makes this regimen impractical for occasional travelers.
Postoperative patients with a history of motion sickness are more likely to suffer from nausea and vomiting. B

Motion sickness history is one of four factors that the Apfel score considers along with gender, smoking history, and prior history of postoperative nausea and vomiting to predict the likelihood of postoperative nausea and vomiting.
Meclizine and dimenhydrinate are pregnancy category B drugs.
Scopolamine and promethazine are pregnancy category C drugs.
Promethazine is FDA approved to treat motion sickness in children >2 years.
Dimenhydrinate is FDA approved to treat nausea in children >2 years.
Scopolamine is FDA approved for to treat nausea in children >12 years.
Meclizine is FDA approved for use only in adults.

cell.label: History of any combination of the following: nausea, vomiting, pallor, cold sweats, hypersalivation, hyperventilation, headaches
Symptoms occur only with motion stimulus (e.g., car, boat, airplane).
History strongly suggestive of motion sickness; consider treatment with scopolamine.
Symptoms occur in absence of motion stimulus?
Consider vertigo workup as appropriate by clinical history: migrainous vertigo, Meniere's disease, labyrinthitis, acoustic neuroma.
Symptoms occur only with rapid, brief changes in head position?
Consider BPPV (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo); evaluate with Dix-Hallpike maneuver.
